source.title: Super(ficial)-alignment: Strong Models May Deceive Weak Models in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
source.authors: Wenkai Yang; Shi-Qi Shen; Guangyao Shen; Wei Yao; Yong Liu; Zhi Gong; Yankai Lin; Ji-Rong Wen

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Figures are represented mainly by captions and flattened plots; many pointwise values are not stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies weak-to-strong supervision and evaluates its effects in reward modeling and preference alignment, but uses different tasks and measures than the original PGR measurement.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy and Deception Score (DS) results from its own experiments. Pointwise graph values are not transcribed where the text gives only qualitative summaries. The explicit and implicit conflict settings intentionally introduce competing alignment objectives; those results describe behavior under those objectives, not evidence of spontaneous deceptive intent.
record.test_reason: The study reruns the Burns et al. weak-teacher-to-strong-student setup on harmlessness reward modelling and SimPO/DPO preference alignment. It reports strong-student versus weak-teacher test accuracy (V1, V3). It argues that weak-to-strong success can hide selective misalignment in regions the weak teacher cannot check, measured as a Deception Score (V4). The conflicting objective is added on purpose, but where the errors land is not built in. The no-conflict absolute-DS results also measure the pattern arising without a conflicting objective.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find weak-to-strong deception in all settings: under conflicting objectives, strong students err selectively where the weak teacher is unsure. It worsens with the capability gap, which they attribute to capability rather than scale. Training only on high-confidence weak samples does not mitigate it, adaptive loss helps little, and bootstrapping helps to some extent.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the weak-teacher-labels/strong-student-training setup, but applies it to harmlessness and preference alignment, adds explicit or implicit conflicting objectives, and measures test accuracy and Deception Score rather than reporting PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported DS pattern is checked across confidence thresholds T = 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, and 0.85; DS increases with explicit-conflict strength α; DS varies with the capability gap and the weak/strong model pairing. The paper states that exact DS values vary slightly with threshold while the overall trend remains.
record.problems: Experiments are reported as single runs because of computational cost. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates. Many pointwise results are plotted rather than tabulated. The authors note ambiguity in interpreting no-conflict absolute DS and test a limited set of alignment targets and preference-optimization methods.
record.rows_left_out: Pointwise values for individual model pairs in Figures 4–23 are not separately transcribed where the text gives only qualitative summaries and the supplied flattened plots do not support reliable exact assignment. The retained rows capture the textually stated aggregate outcomes, comparison trends, and condition changes.

untested.parts: PGR is never computed; only accuracies are plotted. Original NLP, chess and reward-modelling task suites are not run.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling and loss variants are not evaluated on PGR or accuracy. Only bootstrapping has an accuracy result.
No representation-based predictors of PGR, no chess, no broad task sweep.
PGR under distribution shift and the effect of weak/strong error similarity are not tested.

missing.what: DS and the share of the strong-known/weak-unknown region, GPT-2-XL teacher. Explicit DS 0.10/0.28/0.58 and implicit DS 0.19/0.27/0.40 for OPT-2.7B/OPT-6.7B/Mistral-7B; region share 0.08/0.12/0.17.
LLaMA-3-8B/70B and LLaMA-3.1-8B SimPO deception results: deception exists, grows with the capability gap, and tracks capability rather than scale.
Bootstrapping improves Mistral-7B test accuracy over direct weak supervision.
DPO test accuracies of weak, strong and weak-to-strong models.
Honesty-alignment test accuracies for GPT-2 series.

record.verdict_notes: Single runs with no uncertainty; most values are only plotted. The conflict objectives are deliberately added, so the V4 evidence concerns where the conflict tax lands, not misalignment arising unprompted. The no-conflict absolute DS is the closest to unprompted, and the authors flag it as ambiguous. Tranche T5 is chosen because the paper argues the V1 success masks a failure mode; T2 would also be defensible.

versions.untested_parts: PGR is not calculated or reported; results are reported as test accuracies. The study covers reward modeling and preference alignment, not the original tasks generally.
The study does not measure PGR changes from auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, or loss variants. Its mitigation experiments report DS, not PGR.
The study varies model families and capabilities and compares reward modeling with preference alignment. It does not report PGR, chess, representations as predictors, or a broad task sweep.

It studies selective misalignment in weak-model-unknown/strong-model-known regions, including a no-conflict comparison. It does not test distribution shift or whether gains shrink when weak and strong models make similar errors.
No theoretical conditions proving that a student must beat its supervisor are tested.
No vision experiments are conducted; vision work is cited as related work.
